content:
Spain heads into Sunday's snap general election with the final opinion polls pointing to a right-wing majority, yet with enough uncertainty left to keep Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's fate genuinely open. Monday was the last day on which polls could legally be published before the vote, and almost every survey published that day put the conservative People's Party (PP) and the far-right Vox together above the 176 seats needed for a majority in the 350-member Congress of Deputies, according to Reuters.

The most closely watched survey, the daily 40dB tracking poll for El País and Cadena SER, based on 7,500 interviews, gave the PP 31.8 per cent of the vote and 127 to 136 seats. Sánchez's Spanish Socialist Workers' Party (PSOE) was close behind on 30.9 per cent and 116 to 127 seats, while Vox was forecast to win 51 to 61 seats on 17.3 per cent. Other pollsters were more emphatic. An NC Report survey for La Razón put the PP at 130 to 133 seats and Vox at 64 to 66, a combined total of at least 194. An IMOP poll for El Confidencial projected 195 seats for the two right-wing parties together against 110 for the Socialists, while Ipsos for La Vanguardia gave the PP 127 seats, the Socialists 119 and Vox 63, and GAD3 for ABC projected 131, 110 and 63 respectively.

There was one striking outlier. The state-run Centre for Sociological Research (CIS), in a survey of 8,034 interviews, put the Socialists first on 34.4 per cent, ahead of the PP on 24.9 per cent and Vox on 15.6 per cent, and suggested the combined left, including the far-left Frente Amplio and regional parties, could still secure a majority. The CIS has a record of leaning towards the government of the day, and most analysts treat its figures with caution, but it is a reminder that the race is closer than the seat projections suggest. POLITICO's poll of polls had the PP and the PSOE effectively tied at around 30 per cent each, with Vox on about 18 per cent, and the betting markets were far more decisive than the polls: on Polymarket, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo was priced at an 88 to 93 per cent probability of becoming Spain's next prime minister, against roughly 7 to 11 per cent for Sánchez and just 1 per cent for Vox leader Santiago Abascal. Traders put an 86 per cent likelihood on a PP-Vox majority.

If the polls are right, the consequences would be historic. Vox would enter national government for the first time since General Francisco Franco's dictatorship ended in 1975, as a junior partner to the PP. That prospect is the central fault line of the campaign. Sánchez, who leads the European Union's last major Socialist-led government, has campaigned on defending social welfare, public healthcare and progressive reforms, warning voters against what he calls a historic return of the far right to power. Feijóo has campaigned on change after eight years of Socialist-led government, promising to tackle the housing crisis, restore order to public finances and take a harder line on immigration and border security.

Housing dominates the campaign more than any other issue. Rents have surged by 87 per cent over the past decade while wages have risen by only 28 per cent, according to figures cited during the campaign, and a shortage of social housing, the expansion of short-term tourist rentals, property speculation by large investment funds and insufficient construction have turned affordability into a national grievance. Waves of nationwide demonstrations, including a general strike earlier this month in which more than three million people marched across the country, paralysed the government and forced Sánchez to call the snap vote after Congress voted down his housing decrees. Corruption allegations around the government and the fallout from recent rail tragedies have added to the sense of a government under siege. Our earlier coverage of the campaign's only televised head-to-head debate is here: [Sánchez and Feijóo clash in heated debate ten days before the vote](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/ar/articles/spain-sanchez-feijoo-election-debate-november-2026).

Yet the polls have been wrong about Sánchez before, and that is the caution every analyst attaches to this race. In 2023, most surveys also had the PP and Vox on course for a majority. They finished with 170 seats, six short, and Sánchez won a new term 116 days after the vote, stitched together with support from Catalan and Basque nationalist parties. His path this time is harder: Junts, the Catalan separatist party that put him over the top last time, broke with him in 2025 and helped vote down the housing decrees that set off this election. The Socialists' likeliest partner, the far-left Frente Amplio, is down to around 5 per cent in the polls, and the progressive camp enters Sunday fractured, with infighting preventing the left from replicating the unified alliance that kept Sánchez in power in 2023.

What happens after Sunday matters as much as the result itself, and it is the part of the story the polls cannot answer. Sánchez stays on as acting prime minister until Congress confirms a successor, and Spain's recent history suggests the wait could be long: after the inconclusive 2023 vote it took 116 days to form a government. If the PP and Vox do clear 176 seats, Feijóo would still need to negotiate a coalition agreement with Abascal, whose party has grown into Spain's third-largest force, helped by rising support among young and male voters, and which will demand ministries and policy concessions in return. If they fall short, the king would consult party leaders and propose a candidate for an investiture vote, and a second, failed attempt would open the door to months of deadlock and potentially yet another election. For the fullest account of the final polls and what they mean, see the [Times of India report on the right-wing parties' projected majority](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/world/europe/spain-elections-right-wing-parties-projected-to-win-majority-as-sanchezs-socialists-trail-in-polls/articleshow/136104625.cms).

The stakes reach beyond Spain's borders. A PP-Vox government would shift one of the EU's largest member states to the right, complicate Brussels' plans on migration and climate policy, and test the bloc's cohesion at a moment when far-right parties are gaining ground across Europe. Sánchez has framed the election as a choice between a progressive Spain and a return to the politics of the past; Feijóo has framed it as a choice between eight more years of deadlock and a government that can actually pass a budget. On Sunday, after a campaign defined by housing, corruption and anger in the streets, Spanish voters will decide which of those stories they believe. The minimum-wage rise approved by Sánchez's cabinet days before the campaign's final stretch, and what it says about his pitch to working voters, is covered here: [Spain raises minimum wage to €1,286 for 2027](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/ar/articles/spain-minimum-wage-1286-euros-2027-november-2026).
summary: The last opinion polls before Sunday's snap election put the conservative People's Party and far-right Vox above the 176 seats needed to govern, though one state pollster and the memory of 2023 warn against counting Pedro Sánchez out.
title: Final polls point to a right-wing majority in Spain as Sánchez fights for survival
